episodes.192155: A pre-frontal trough axis moving into a moderately unstable atmosphere over southern middle Tennessee produced strong to severe thunderstorms over Lincoln, Moore, and Franklin counties in Tennessee during the mid afternoon hours. Franklin county was hit with winds between 60 and 65 mph.
episodes.192481: The monsoon high slid east of NM over TX bringing monsoon moisture northward into NM. Slow steering flow coupled with moisture allowed for two more days of burn scar flash flooding on the complex of burn scars in and around Ruidoso. The first of which caused only a minor road closure near Mechem Drive. The second of which was far more widespread bringing impacts from Alto to Ruidoso to Ruidoso Downs.
episodes.192575: A deep moisture profile and an increase of deep-layer shear over Central Alabama on July 28 resulted in very efficient rainfall occurring over central and northern parts of the region. Precipitable water values of 2.1 to 2.2 inches aided high instantaneous rain rates, at times on the order of 5-7 in/hr. Sporadic flooding occurred in Marion County during the early afternoon as two rounds of heavy rainfall moved through the area. By late afternoon, training thunderstorms over the Cahaba Heights area quickly flooded area homes and streets before another, much larger, round of thunderstorms overtook Jefferson County from the west. Many of the southern and western suburbs of Birmingham experienced flooding of homes and roadways during the early evening hours as 3-5 inches of rain fell across these areas.||The next day, an MCS tracking into northeast Alabama from Tennessee resulted in several trees being blown down in Cherokee County, especially the Centre and Cedar Bluff areas.
episodes.192583: Warm and humid conditions with dewpoints in the low 70s fueled an early evening cluster of thunderstorms southwest of Indianapolis.  A moist profile promoted efficient rainfall production, with resultant bands of torrential downpours training from northeast of Gosport into far west-central Morgan County.
episodes.192666: A large storm trekking across western into southern portions of the state crossed through Jones county with up to tennis-ball sized hail and damaging winds. The Jones county sheriff reported several hail damaged vehicles on Interstate 90, and that strong winds had flipped over some campers and knocked over motorcyclists. A CoCoRaHS observer 12 miles west of Murdo measured the hail at 2.5 inches. While other storms were in the area, few other reports of severe weather occurred with these storms, with the most notable being the weather station 2 miles north of Harreid (Campbell county) recording a wind gust of 70 mph. USDA crop indemnities for Jones county topped 188 thousand dollars.
episodes.192706: Scattered thunderstorms impacted Middle Tennessee on July 29, 2024. The most impactful thunderstorm of the day was located in the Murfreesboro area. A microburst with estimated 80 mph winds caused tree and structural damage in the area. Meanwhile, an EF-0 tornado touched down on Middle Tennessee State University's campus.
episodes.192779: An upper longwave trough paired with weak shortwaves brings clusters of thunderstorms to the South. One cluster produces a couple instances of severe damaging winds in East Tennessee.
episodes.192794: A band of strong thunderstorms developed across west-central Illinois during the pre-dawn hours of July 29th, then tracked eastward toward the I-55 corridor by mid-morning.  Some of the cells produced damaging wind gusts of around 60 mph and scattered wind damage in portions of Schuyler and Fulton counties.
episodes.193650: A vigorous tropical wave, the one that later became Tropical Cyclone Debby, moved near Puerto Rico by the end of July. This wave, along with other weaker trade wind disturbances, led to strong showers and thunderstorms, that resulted in flooding in San Juan, Aguada, Patillas, and Comerio.
episodes.193777: Severe thunderstorms over southern South Dakota, tracked into the eastern half of Boyd and far northeastern Holt county during the early morning hours of July 29th. Hail up to ping pong size was reported.
episodes.193802: As a surface frontal boundary pushed southward through the southeastern United States, winds began to veer south-southeast bringing moist, warm air into South Florida. This supported the development of numerous showers and thunderstorms along the sea-breeze on the afternoon and evening of July 29th.
episodes.193846: Modest instability under an upper level area of low pressure in the afternoon of July 29th developed a few isolated thunderstorms, including one in Rutland county that produced slightly larger than quarter size hail in Clarendon.
episodes.193968: In the late afternoon of the 28th, a few storms began to fire. One storm, northwest of St. Francis, grew rapidly and stayed strong over the next several hours as it moved southeast. It produced baseball sized hail and estimated winds of 80 MPH which caused property damage.
episodes.194054: The remains of an MCV that tracked across Nebraska earlier in the day moved into Iowa in the late afternoon. These remnants moved into a deeply unstable environment with 2000+ J/kg of SBCAPE and intensified through the early evening, transitioning to a loosely organized bowing segment in the evening. Steep mid and low level lapse rates and DCAPE of 750-1000 J/kg were also available. This combination resulted in a handful of hail and damaging wind gusts across the area.  Heavy rain also occurred as a line of training convection developed behind the bowing segment lasting late into the night. A swath of 3 to 5 inches of rain occurred with the system in central to southern Iowa, however no flood impacts were noted.
episodes.194098: A scattered line of storms moved into central Kansas from northwest Kansas during the late evening hours. One stronger storm produced wind gusts up to 67 mph in Russell County.
episodes.194146: A line of severe thunderstorms with strong wind gusts developed across central and southern portions of Campbell County and tracked east into southern Crook and Weston counties.
episodes.194152: A line of severe thunderstorms moved out of Wyoming and across the northern Black Hills area before weakening as it moved onto the plains. The storms produced wind gusts to over 70 mph.
episodes.194155: A thunderstorm became severe over the central foothills, near Hermosa, and tracked east onto the adjacent plains before weakening east of the Black Hills. The storm produced hail to over golf ball size.
episodes.194156: A short-lived severe storm developed over Bennett County, producing large hail and wind gusts to over 70 mph.
episodes.194157: A large supercell thunderstorm developed over southern Haakon County and tracked east-southeast across south central South Dakota. The storm produced large hail and damaging wind gusts across the area, including significant damage in the Winner area.
episodes.194158: Thunderstorms over northwest South Dakota formed into a line over Perkins County, producing wind gusts to around 60 mph.
episodes.194159: A supercell thunderstorm developed along the South Dakota and Nebraska border in south central South Dakota and tracked eastward across the area. There was a report of quarter sized hail east of Lakeview.
episodes.194180: Isolated early morning thunderstorms brought hail to the size of quarters and strong winds to portions of central and north central South Dakota. A peak wind gust of 60 mph was observed by the DOT weather station 5 miles west northwest of Mclaughlin, and wind driven hail was responsible for damaging siding to a residence 3 miles north northeast of Iona.
episodes.194235: An isolated severe thunderstorm developed in the early morning hours of July 29th and produced damaging winds.
episodes.194395: Training heavy rainfall developed in portions of Southern Illinois during the evening hours on the 28th, with flash flooding developing in Wayne and Saline Counties. Eldorado was hit hard for a second time with rainfall totals around 5 inches, prompting water rescues. Water intruded into buildings including the Ferrell Hospital, which had already been heavily impacted from a flood in May. PW values were up to 2 inches.
episodes.194602: A strong instability plume set up across the southeastern half of AZ with MLCAPE values upwards of 1000 J/KG. Simultaneously, an upper-level trough moving across the Pacific Northwest resulted in a corridor of strong vertical ascent. The combination of the available instability and upper-level forcing resulted in widespread thunderstorm development across southeast AZ with some of the activity moving into portions of southern Gila County, where heavy rainfall was observed across Gilson Wash, west of the San Carlos area. Doppler radar estimated rainfall amounts were in excess of an inch in less than hour, enough to result in water rises along Gilson Wash and flooding along the low-water crossings.
episodes.194656: Broken remnants of an MCS moved out of the Midwest towards the Southeast. A few storms within the system were able to produce damaging wind gusts along an extended length. A few thunderstorms ahead of the line also developed which were also capable of strong to damaging winds.
episodes.194678: Low near Elkhart was in place with an inverted trough extending northward into Nebraska was the focus area as an isolated supercell moved across northern Trego and much of Ellis county between 10 and 11 pm.  Law Enforcement reported that power pole lines were downed from the Thunderstorm winds in the Hays area. Gusts to 61 mph were reported measured by the Public on the southwest side of Hays.
episodes.194691: An isolated thunderstorm became severe as it passed through Grant and Sioux counties, producing estimated 60 mph wind gusts.
episodes.194693: Thunderstorms initially formed in the late afternoon in the vicinity of a surface boundary over southwest North Dakota, with additional storms then forming through the late afternoon into the evening in an environment of elevated instability and deep layer shear. Many storms became supercells, producing very large hail. Over the Bismarck-Mandan area, three separate storms produced large hail. The first storm passed through the Harmon Lake area before crossing the Missouri River and passing through the north side of Bismarck, causing extensive damage with hail up to 3 inches in diameter. As that storm moved along, a second storm formed to the south of Mandan and quickly intensified as it crossed the Missouri River and passed over developments to the south of Bismarck and over the Lincoln area. Many locations experienced two inch diameter hail with this storm, which increased to baseball size over Lincoln. One mile south of Lincoln, a hailstone was measured at 4.5 inches. These two storms caused extensive damage to structures and vehicles, resulting in millions of dollars in damage. A third severe storm then formed over Bismarck, but this storm was weaker, producing one-inch diameter hail. Additional thunderstorms then continued over central North Dakota with the main threat shifting towards strong winds late in the event. The strongest wind gust was estimated at 75 mph at McKenna Lake, near Napoleon, Logan County, where four campers were blown over.
episodes.194771: During the evening hours on July 29th, a line of storms moved through portions of western Wisconsin. As these storms moved through Richland County, tree damage was reported.
episodes.194835: Scattered thunderstorms developed along a stationary surface boundary which was across northern MN to eastern SD. Most of the thunderstorms were sub-severe, however a few did produce periods of heavy rainfall and strong wind gusts. A few trees were downed in Yellow Medicine and Wright Counties.
episodes.195016: Unusually moist airmass ahead of an approaching mesolow and lake breezes led to development of efficient rain-producing showers and storms in the late afternoon...leading to rainfall rates near two and a half inches per hour at times. Storm total rainfall by the next morning was largely between 1 and locally as high as 4-6 inches.
episodes.195051: Thunderstorms developed along a weak boundary during the evening with up to 2000 J/kg MUCAPE and increasing deep-layer shear as a mid-level wind maxima approached from western Nebraska and southwest South Dakota. The strongest storm produced up to baseball size hail.
episodes.195127: A Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) comprised of strong to severe thunderstorms moved southeast from central Tennessee into northern Alabama during the mid-afternoon hours on the 29th. Additional clusters of storms that developed ahead of this MCS merged with this activity in a moderately unstable atmosphere. This ended up producing a more defined MCS as it moved into Alabama, producing a large area of damaging winds in southeastern Jackson and northeastern DeKalb counties.
episodes.195183: The prevailing upper-level pattern for the end of July featured a trough over the Pacific Northwest, favoring southwesterly flow over the central Great Plains. Two troughs ejected out into the north-central CONUS during this episode. The first brought two back to back nights of severe weather across portions of northeast Nebraska the night of the 28th and the 29th. The second trough moved out into the central Plains and brought the synoptic scale forcing for a historic severe wind event that impacted both Lincoln and Omaha metropolitan areas. Wind gusts as high as 100 miles per hour extended from Lancaster County northeast to the Nebraska-Iowa border, leaving behind a large swath of significant tree, powerline and structural damage. Power outages from this storm lasted for up to a week in some locations, particularly in Omaha.||This episode also featured several afternoons of excessive heat for portions of southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa. A few instances of 110 degree heat indices were observed in a few southwest Iowa counties the afternoon of the 29th, with even more widespread excessive heat the afternoon of the 31st across much of the forecast area south of Interstate 80. Peak heat indices in this region topped out between 110 and 115 degrees before afternoon convection cooled temperatures back down.
episodes.195351: A couple of thunderstorms produced sporadic damaging wind gusts and a little hail near the DC and Baltimore metro areas.

Rainfall amounts of 0.50 to 1.50 inches fell on the South Fork burn scar west of downtown Ruidoso during the early afternoon hours. This rainfall resulted in more burn scar flash flooding and debris flows across neighborhoods in Alto and Ruidoso. The Cherokee Mobile Village along U.S. Highway 70 at the Lincoln and Otero County line was evacuated due to flash flooding. Mechem Dr. became impassible again due to Cedar Creek overflowing its banks and rushing over the roadway. Heavy flows along Cedar Creek caused Mechem Dr. to become impassable, washed out a part of Musket Ball Dr. and brought debris flow over Cree Meadows Drive. Flooding of the Rio Ruidoso resulted in the closure of Gavilan Canyon Road and the evacuation of the Gavilan Mobile Home Park. Debris flow on the Rio Ruidoso destroyed a culvert on the eastern end of the Ruidoso Downs racetrack. Water and debris flow reported west of Alto making NM 532 impassable. Fortunately, no reports of significant water rises were received downstream of the water breach at Ruidoso Downs. Culvert and trailer park damage cost is an estimate.

A small, weak EF-0 tornado moved through Murfreesboro, also impacting Middle Tennessee State University. Main damage was large tree branches down with some trees uprooted. Minor structural damage was noted at the stadium, including some siding material off of one of the buildings and some gate and fencing damage. The tornado began just east of Memorial Boulevard, continued east-southeast towards Middle Tennessee State University, and ended southeast of campus on Copper Hollow Drive. Maximum winds were estimated to be 75 mph. Damages are a rough estimate.

Damage consisted of many trees down or uprooted, many branches snapped off, and some structural damage, primarily due to trees or branches falling. There was some minor roof damage to a few buildings, including metal peeled up at a business and some shingles lost on a few houses. Damages are a rough estimate.

Most locations initially experienced hail ranging from one to two inches in diameter, but as the storm approached Lincoln hail increased to baseball size. In addition, one mile to the south of Lincoln a hailstone was measured at 4.5 inches in diameter.
